description:
🇫🇷 (English version below)

On créera une carte interactive de Mars pour les futurs astronautes ! 🚀 On aime l'informatique, coder et créer des logiciels. On cherche des gens motivés, dynamiques et cool pour échanger des idées, apprendre et relever ce défi ensemble !

English

We're building a Mars map for future astronauts! 🚀 We love coding and building software. Looking for curious, motivated, energetic and friendly teammates to share ideas and create something awesome together!
summary:
We built Marswalk Budget, a planner for the first astronauts who will walk on Mars. You pick the rocks you want to visit at Gale Crater or Jezero Crater, and it finds the easiest path across real rover terrain. Then it tells you what the walk costs: how long it takes, how much suit oxygen you burn, how much radiation you pick up, and how much science you bring back. Every stop shows a real photo that Curiosity or Perseverance took there.
The part we cared about most is getting home. The map marks the point of no return, and if a dust storm hits or the sample bag gets heavy, it redoes the plan and tells you which stops to drop. The same plan then goes on a field tablet, a helmet display and a phone VR headset.
Most Mars maps show where things are. We wanted one that shows what each place costs before you go.
details:
The three pictures above: a walk that fits the budget at Gale Crater, the same walk after a dust storm hits (NO-GO, turn back by T+3:29, and a smaller plan that still fits), and the helmet display the astronaut follows outside.

How you use it
Open the site and pick a crater. Click the stops you want on the map, which shows HiRISE imagery, the rover's real drive path and the terrain. The planner draws a route, and a card shows the walking time, oxygen used, radiation dose and a science score. Every stop has a photo the rover took nearby and a short note on why it matters, with its NASA source. At Gale we also show the APXS rock chemistry measured at that spot.
Then make things worse. Turn on a dust storm, a solar storm or a heavy sample kit and it replans. If the walk no longer fits, you get a NO-GO, a red marker where you have to turn back, and a smaller set of stops that still fits. You can also compare three versions of the same walk: least oxygen, gentler ground, and shortest.

How it works
We turned real elevation data into a grid of 5 m squares. Walking from one square to the next costs energy depending on the slope, the ground and how much you carry, and an A* search finds the cheapest path between stops. We convert that energy into oxygen, and time outside into radiation dose using what Curiosity's RAD instrument measured on the surface. Slopes steeper than 20° are off limits (from a NASA lunar EVA study), and 20% of the 0.5 kg oxygen supply is kept as a reserve. We checked the oxygen model against NASA's Life Support Baseline Values and Assumptions Document (BVAD, 2018): it lists 0.075 kg of oxygen per hour for a spacewalk, and our walk at Gale averages 0.074 kg per hour.

Backup plans
Sometimes the walk is just too long. A supply cache on the route lets the astronaut refill oxygen once, and a storm shelter counts as a safe place, so the point of no return is measured to the nearest refuge, not only to the habitat. These are hypothetical sites, one of each per crater. With the cache, the Gale walk that failed in a dust storm with a heavy kit fits again. You can also switch to a pressurized rover: it drives between stops, the crew suit up at each one, and the planner checks the walk-back limit Apollo used. If the rover broke down anywhere on the drive, could they walk home on the oxygen in their suits?

Taking it outside
A plan is only useful if the astronaut can follow it. The same plan opens on a field tablet, a helmet HUD that counts oxygen and dose as you walk, a 3D fly-through, and a split-screen VR view for a phone headset.

What we used
Plain HTML, CSS and JavaScript, with Leaflet for the map and three.js for 3D. No framework and no build step. Node.js runs our data preparation and about 120 tests that work offline.

What isn't perfect yet
This is a student prototype, not a flight tool. The radiation rate was measured at Gale, so at Jezero it is a stand-in. The weather is archival (Perseverance MEDA sol 1133, Curiosity REMS sol 4995), and the solar storm alerts come from DONKI, which watches near Earth, not Mars. The slope limit comes from a Moon study and the walking model from research on Earth. The science scores are our own choices. Every number we had to assume is tagged ASSUMPTION in the code and explained, with its source, in docs/model.md.
